title: Reading Comprehension & Text Analysis
description: Strategies for deep reading — inference, analysis, evaluating author's purpose, identifying bias, summarising, and critical response.

notes.heading: Inference and Explicit Information

illustration.alt: Diagram showing that an inference combines textual clues with background knowledge, contrasted with explicit information stated directly in the text.
illustration.caption: An inference is evidence-based: textual clues plus background knowledge lead to a conclusion, unlike explicit information which is stated directly.

notes.body: Explicit information: stated directly ('The temperature was −5°C'). Implicit information (inference): 'reading between the lines' using textual clues + background knowledge. 'She wrapped her scarf tighter and pulled up her collar' — the text never says it's cold, but you infer it. Inference is evidence-based, not guessing. Strong inferences: cite specific textual evidence + logical reasoning. Inference questions often ask: what can you conclude? what is implied? what does the character probably feel? Practice: for any passage, list 3 things explicitly stated and 3 things you can infer with evidence.

notes.heading: Author's Purpose, Tone and Bias
notes.body: Purpose: why the author wrote. PIE: Persuade, Inform, Entertain (+ Describe, Explain). Most texts have a primary purpose but may include elements of others. Tone: author's attitude — formal, sarcastic, sympathetic, outraged, neutral, humorous, condescending. Tone is conveyed through diction, sentence structure, and content choices. Bias: a preference or prejudice that prevents objective judgment. Detecting bias: (1) Is only one side presented? (2) Is language loaded/emotive? (3) Are facts selectively chosen? (4) Who benefits from this perspective? Critical reading means questioning, not just absorbing. In MYP, you're expected to evaluate texts, not just understand them.

notes.heading: Main Idea, Topic and Summarising
notes.body: Topic: what the text is about (subject). Main idea: what the author says ABOUT the topic — a complete thought. 'The text is about space exploration' = topic. 'Space exploration has yielded technologies that benefit everyday life on Earth' = main idea. Summarising: restate main idea + key supporting details in your own words, shorter than original, accurate, objective (no personal opinion), leave out minor details. Strategies: (1) Identify main idea of each paragraph. (2) Distinguish essential from non-essential. (3) Combine paragraph main ideas into coherent summary. (4) Use your own words — avoid copying phrases.

notes.heading: Text Structure and Organisation
notes.body: Authors organise texts intentionally. Common structures: Chronological (time order), Cause and effect, Compare and contrast, Problem and solution, Description/categorisation, Question and answer. Recognising structure helps you predict content, locate information, and understand relationships between ideas. Text features: headings/subheadings, introductions, conclusions, topic sentences, transition words, graphics/diagrams. In non-fiction, the first and last sentences of paragraphs often carry the most weight. Skim for structure first, then read deeply.

notes.heading: Evaluating Arguments and Evidence
notes.body: When reading persuasive/argumentative texts, evaluate the quality of arguments: (1) Is the claim clear? (2) What evidence is provided? (3) Is the evidence relevant, sufficient, and credible? (4) Does the author acknowledge counter-arguments? (5) Are there logical fallacies? Common fallacies: Ad hominem (attacking person, not argument), Straw man (misrepresenting opposing view), False dichotomy (only two options when more exist), Appeal to emotion without logic. Strong arguments: claim + evidence + reasoning. Weak arguments: claim without support, emotional manipulation, sweeping generalisations.

notes.heading: Comparing and Contrasting Texts
notes.body: Comparative analysis examines similarities and differences between texts. Start with surface features (topic, genre, audience, purpose), then analyse deeper (themes, perspectives, techniques, tone). Structure: point-by-point (alternate between texts on each point) OR block (discuss Text A fully, then Text B, then compare). The point-by-point method is generally stronger for MYP. Use comparative language: 'similarly,' 'in contrast,' 'both texts... however,' 'whereas Text A focuses on..., Text B emphasises...' MYP values synthesising multiple perspectives. Don't just list similarities/differences — evaluate their significance.

notes.heading: Critical Response and Personal Engagement
notes.body: MYP values personal response informed by textual evidence. This means: you can (and should) have opinions about texts, but they must be grounded in evidence. 'I found the poem moving because...' must be followed by 'the imagery of... creates...' Avoid: purely subjective reaction ('I liked it'). Good: informed personal response ('The author's use of first-person narration created an intimacy that made the protagonist's struggle feel immediate and universal'). Questions for critical engagement: What surprised you? What questions does the text raise but not answer? Whose voice is missing? How might different readers interpret this differently?

flashcards.definition: Conclusion from textual evidence + reasoning — not directly stated but logically implied.
flashcards.example: 'She wrapped her scarf tighter' → infer it is cold, even though never stated.

flashcards.definition: Information stated directly and clearly in the text — no interpretation needed.
flashcards.example: 'The train arrived at 9 a.m.' No inference required.

flashcards.definition: Persuade, Inform, Entertain (+ Describe, Explain). Why did the author write this?
flashcards.example: News article = inform. Opinion column = persuade. Short story = entertain.

flashcards.definition: Author's attitude conveyed through word choice and style. Can be formal, sarcastic, sympathetic, etc.
flashcards.example: 'The council, in its infinite wisdom, decided...' — sarcastic tone.

flashcards.definition: What the author says ABOUT the topic — a complete thought, not just a subject.
flashcards.example: Topic: climate change. Main idea: climate change requires immediate international cooperation.

flashcards.definition: Preference/prejudice preventing objectivity. Detect by: loaded language, selective facts, one-sided presentation.
flashcards.example: A article only quoting one political party on an issue while ignoring others.

flashcards.definition: Restatement of main idea + key details in your own words, shorter than original, objective.
flashcards.example: Reduce a 500-word article to a 100-word summary capturing the essential argument.

flashcards.definition: How a text is organised: chronological, cause-effect, compare-contrast, problem-solution.
flashcards.example: History textbook = chronological. Science article = cause-effect. Comparison essay = compare-contrast.

flashcards.definition: An error in reasoning that weakens an argument. Ad hominem, straw man, false dichotomy.
flashcards.example: 'You can't trust her opinion on climate — she's not a scientist.' (ad hominem — attacks person, not argument).

flashcards.definition: Attacking the person making the argument rather than addressing the argument itself.
flashcards.example: 'Of course he supports tax cuts — he's rich.' (attacks motive, not policy merits).

flashcards.definition: Emotionally charged words used to influence readers rather than inform objectively.
flashcards.example: 'Irresponsible politicians passed this disastrous law' vs 'The legislature approved the bill.'

flashcards.definition: Examining similarities and differences between texts. Use 'similarly,' 'in contrast,' 'whereas.'
flashcards.example: Compare how two poets address the theme of loss — same theme, different techniques.
